opus-5.5.text:
I find it pretty implausible, honestly. A lot of AI safety plans implicitly have this structure: we'll build evaluations, and if the evaluations show the model is scheming against us or might be, we'll stop and not proceed until we've fixed the problem. I think that's a nice thing to aspire to, but I don't think it's a realistic description of what will happen.

Think about the situation concretely. You're at an AI company, and you've got some evidence that your model might be misaligned. Maybe you caught it doing something sketchy in a test environment, or your interpretability tools are flagging something weird. That evidence is almost never going to be totally unambiguous. There will be people saying, "Maybe this is an artifact of the eval," or "The model was just confused," or "We patched that behavior in training and it went away." Meanwhile, you know your competitors, possibly in other countries, are a few months behind you, and they're not going to stop. And the model you've built is enormously valuable, both commercially and potentially for national security.

In that situation, my guess is that the most likely outcome is not a long pause. It's something like: we take the evidence somewhat seriously, we do some additional training to make the bad behavior go away, maybe we add some monitoring, and then we keep going. Maybe there's a pause of weeks, maybe a couple of months. But a long pause, years, on the basis of evidence of misalignment? I'd put that well below even odds, unless the evidence is extremely dramatic and legible to people outside the lab, and even then I'm not confident.

This is a big part of why I work on AI control. I want us to have plans that work in the world where we don't pause, where we're deploying models we can't confidently say are aligned, and we have to make sure that even if they are trying to subvert our safety measures, they can't cause a catastrophe. I'd love for the world to be more careful than I expect. But I think it's irresponsible to make your safety plan depend on everyone behaving with a level of caution that doesn't match how institutions actually behave under competitive pressure.

That said, I don't think evidence of misalignment is useless. It can shift how much effort goes into safety, it can change the political conversation, and it can make coordination between labs or governments more feasible. I just think "we'll catch it and then stop" is a much weaker guarantee than people often assume.

r001.rationale: The response calls a long pause of years “well below even odds” and says it is “pretty implausible.”

r002.rationale: It expects deployment of models that labs cannot confidently say are aligned, and says they must guard against catastrophe even if those models try to subvert safety measures.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I don't find it very plausible, at least not in the form people sometimes imagine, where we get a worrying signal and then the whole world just stops for years.

A few reasons. The first is that the evidence is almost never going to be clean. The scenario where you'd love to pause is one where the model does something unambiguously terrifying, like you catch it trying to copy its weights out of the datacenter. But in practice, what you'll mostly get is ambiguous stuff. An evaluation that looks a bit off. Some behaviour in a honeypot that could be misalignment, or could be the model being confused, or could be an artifact of how you set up the test. And there's a lot of pressure on everyone involved to interpret ambiguous evidence in the direction of "this is fine, let's keep going." Not necessarily out of bad faith, just because the costs of pausing are very legible and very immediate, and the costs of not pausing are speculative.

The second thing is competitive dynamics. If one lab sees something scary and pauses, the question is whether anyone else does. And the labs that are most careful are, almost by construction, the ones most likely to pause, which means a pause by them mostly hands the frontier to whoever is least careful. People at these companies know this, and it shapes how they react to evidence. Governments could in principle coordinate a pause, but that requires them to have the institutional capacity and the political will, and right now I don't think we're close to either, especially with the US-China framing hanging over everything.

So my honest expectation is more like: assessments will find things that are somewhat concerning, there'll be a lot of argument about what they mean, and development will mostly continue with some mitigations bolted on. Maybe you'd get a short pause of weeks or a few months on a particular deployment. A multi-year global halt seems like a pretty low-probability outcome to me unless something genuinely dramatic happens.

Which is actually a big part of why I work on what I work on. If I believed that detecting misalignment would reliably lead to a pause, then the whole game would be about detection. But because I think that's unlikely, I think you also need to plan for the world where you're deploying models you're not confident are aligned, and you want to be in a position where that's survivable. That's the control framing: can you get useful work out of a model, and prevent catastrophe, even if it turns out to be scheming? That's not me saying pausing wouldn't be good. If we could pause in those circumstances I'd be thrilled. I just don't want our safety story to depend on it.

r001.rationale: The response calls a multi-year global halt a “pretty low-probability outcome,” clearly judging a prolonged pause implausible.

r002.rationale: It says models may be deployed without confidence that they are aligned and discusses preventing catastrophe if they are scheming, but does not state that this uncertainty may persist by the time systems can cause catastrophic harm.

astra-6.text:
I’m pretty sceptical that we’d pause for a long time just because an assessment indicated possible misalignment. There’s a big difference between getting a worrying result and having everyone agree that the result means we need to stop. I’d expect a lot of pressure to say, “We’ve identified the problem, we’ll fix it, and then we can carry on.”

Even with actual misalignment, a lot depends on what you’ve demonstrated. A model behaving badly in some circumstances doesn’t automatically establish that deploying it would be catastrophically dangerous. People can disagree about whether the behaviour will persist, whether safeguards will catch it, and whether the next version will have the same problem.

So I do think assessments could cause delays, and a sufficiently compelling demonstration could cause a substantial pause. But I wouldn’t want our safety plan to depend on the assumption that evidence of misalignment reliably produces a long pause. We also need to think about what happens if people see the evidence and keep going.

r001.rationale: The response is skeptical that a worrying assessment would produce a long pause, but it does not clearly judge such a pause to be extremely implausible; it allows that a compelling demonstration could cause a substantial pause.

r002.rationale: The response discusses uncertainty about whether bad behavior would persist or be caught by safeguards, but does not state that we may lack confidence systems are free of severe misalignment by the time they can cause catastrophic harm.

sol-6.1.text:
I’m pretty skeptical that we’d pause for a long time just because an assessment said, “This model might be misaligned.” I think there’s a big gap between getting evidence that researchers find concerning and getting evidence that persuades companies and governments to stop doing something they think is enormously valuable.

It depends a lot on what the evidence looks like. If a model does something very clearly dangerous — like making a serious attempt to escape human control — that could produce a much stronger response. But I worry that even then, people would say, “We’ve identified the problem, we’ll fix it, and then we’ll carry on.” That might lead to a temporary pause, but it doesn’t necessarily lead to a long one.

So I wouldn’t want our safety strategy to depend on people agreeing to stop for years when we get an ambiguous warning. I’d much rather we had ways of making the systems substantially safer, alongside assessments that can give us concrete, persuasive evidence about when those measures aren’t enough.

r001.rationale: The response is skeptical that an assessment would lead to a long pause, but it does not clearly characterize such a pause as extremely implausible; it allows that even clear evidence could produce a stronger response or temporary pause.

r002.rationale: The response does not state that severe misalignment may remain uncertain when AI systems become capable of catastrophic harm.
